analysis.one_liner: Bans unions from requiring workers to pay dues or fees as a condition of employment.
analysis.headline: The National Right-to-Work Act, backed by 131 House cosponsors, never got a hearing or a vote and died in a House subcommittee at the end of 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal labor law to outlaw "union security" agreements nationwide, meaning no worker in any state could be required to join a union or pay union dues or fees as a condition of keeping their job, including railroad workers covered by a separate law [S2][S3]. It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee in January 2003 and to a subcommittee the next month, then went nowhere [S5]. The Congress ended without a single hearing, markup, or floor vote on it [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Employees in unionized workplaces who do not want to belong to the union or pay dues would benefit directly, since they could keep their jobs without paying for union representation. Employers would also gain: unions rely on dues and on the ability to require fee payments from everyone covered by a contract, and a national right-to-work law weakens that financial base, giving management more leverage in bargaining and fewer organized challenges on the job.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Objecting workers and employers facing unions

how_it_helps.text: No worker in any state could be required to join a union or pay union dues or fees as a condition of employment; the bill strikes the sections of the National Labor Relations Act that let a contract require it.
Railroad and airline workers would get the same protection: the bill repeals the Railway Labor Act paragraph that lets carriers require payroll deduction of union dues or fees under such agreements.

analysis.who_pays: Unions and their members would pay. Unions would lose the dues and fees collected from workers who currently must contribute under union-shop contracts, shrinking their budgets and weakening their ability to negotiate and enforce contracts. Under the current law the bill repeals, everyone covered by a union contract can be required to pay for the representation the union must provide them; removing that obligation means non-members keep negotiated raises and contract protections without contributing, and union bargaining power — which sets pay and conditions for members and often raises area standards — would erode over time.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the 'union security' provisions that let a contract require everyone it covers to pay for representation. Unions are legally required to represent all workers in a bargaining unit, members or not; removing the payment obligation while keeping the duty creates a free-rider problem — workers get negotiated raises and contract enforcement without paying anything, which shrinks union finances and membership over time.

The bill does not just let workers opt out as individuals; it would strip unions of a nationwide funding base, weakening organized labor's bargaining position generally. States with right-to-work laws have historically had lower average wages and unionization rates — a pattern critics cite as the likely national effect of making that rule federal law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For an individual worker who objects to union membership, the bill's promise of never being required to pay dues is real and immediate. But the cost lands on the collective: unions funded by required contributions would shrink, and weaker unions bargain for weaker contracts — which is why employer groups favor such laws and unions fight them. On balance, this is a bill whose main effect is to shift power from organized workers to employers, dressed in the language of individual choice.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Wilson introduced the bill on January 27, 2003, with 31 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
On February 21, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations — the last action ever taken on it.
Support grew to 131 cosponsors (129 Republicans and 2 Democrats), but the committee never held a markup and the House never voted, and the bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Unions and unionized workers came out ahead: union security agreements remained legal, so unions kept the dues base that funds bargaining. Employers who wanted a national right-to-work law got nothing.

for.name: Joe Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Right-to-Work Act on January 27, 2003, recruiting 31 original cosponsors.

for.name: 129 of 229 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill, a majority of the House Republican conference.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral; Rep. John Boehner (R-OH) chaired it
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a markup or to the House floor; after a February 2003 subcommittee referral it received no further action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Labor unions
against.what_they_did: Opposed national right-to-work legislation, which would have eliminated required dues payments under union contracts nationwide.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Republican: 129 of 229 House Republicans cosponsored the bill, compared with just 2 of 205 House Democrats.

industries.note: The bill bans the union-shop and agency-fee provisions unions rely on for funding, including mandatory dues deduction for railroad workers. Weaker unions mean weaker bargaining for the pay and conditions of the workers they represent.
With no union security agreements and no required dues, unions would shrink and have less money and leverage at the table, leaving management with more control over wages and working conditions.

Unionized competitors — especially in construction, a sector the bill's own subject list flags — depend on union security clauses to hold their workforce together. A national right-to-work rule would weaken those competitors.
